n: As the wall rises, so does the opposition. Sanballat’s first weapon is ridicule — mockery meant to make the builders feel foolish and give up.

f.g: Angry.
Became furious.

n: In front of Samaria’s soldiers, Sanballat fires off scornful questions: Can these weak Jews really finish? Can they bring burned stones back to life? Burned limestone often crumbles, so his taunt had a sting of truth.

f.g: Weak, withered.
Make usable again the fire-damaged stones from the Babylonian destruction.

n: Tobiah adds a joke: the wall is so flimsy a fox could knock it over. Critics often attack the worth of the work as well as the workers.

f.g: Even a light animal like a fox (or jackal) would topple it — a sarcastic insult.

n: Instead of answering the mockers, Nehemiah turns to God in prayer, asking Him to turn their insults back on them.

f.w: turn their reproach upon their own head

n: His prayer is strong, like some of the Psalms, asking God not to overlook their sin. The enemies were not just insulting builders — they were fighting against God’s work.
The result: the wall reaches half its height all the way around, because “the people had a mind to work.” Unity and willing hearts did what mockery said was impossible.

f.w: the people had a mind to work
f.g: Literally “the people had a heart to work” — they were wholehearted.
To half its full height, all around the city.

n: Now Jerusalem is surrounded by enemies on every side: Samaria in the north, Arabs in the south, Ammon in the east, and Ashdod (the old Philistine region) in the west.

f.g: People of Ashdod, a former Philistine city on the coast west of Judah.
Gaps or holes in the wall.

n: Mockery turns to a conspiracy to attack and stop the work by force.
Nehemiah’s response shows a pattern: pray, and post guards. Faith and practical action work together.

f.w: we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch

n: Then discouragement spreads inside Judah. The workers are exhausted, the rubble seems endless, and they fear they cannot finish. In Hebrew this verse sounds like a short, sad work chant.

f.g: Those carrying away rubble and carrying in materials.
Failing, giving out.

n: Meanwhile the enemies plan a surprise attack to kill the builders and end the work.
Jews living in nearby towns come again and again to warn of attack from every direction. “Ten times” means repeatedly; fear can spread through constant rumors.

f.g: An idiom for “over and over.”

n: Nehemiah stations armed families at the lowest, weakest points behind the wall and on the high places, where enemies could see them ready. Families guarding together had every reason to stand firm.

f.g: Arranged by family groups.

n: Nehemiah encourages them: don’t fear — remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your families and homes. Remembering God is the cure for fear.

f.w: fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses

n: Once the enemies realize their plot is known, they back off. Nehemiah sees God’s hand in this, and everyone goes back to work.

f.g: Frustrated their plan, made it come to nothing.

n: From then on, half of Nehemiah’s men work while the other half stand guard in armor, with leaders backing them up.

f.g: Coats of armor, chain mail.
Worked.

n: Carriers work with one hand and hold a weapon with the other. It is a vivid picture of building God’s kingdom while staying on guard against what would destroy it.

f.g: Loaded others with burdens.

f.w: with the other hand held a weapon

n: Each builder wears a sword while working. A trumpeter stays at Nehemiah’s side, ready to sound the alarm.

f.g: Fastened at his waist.
The shofar, a ram’s horn, used to call people together or sound alarm.

n: Nehemiah explains the danger: the wall is long and workers are spread thin.

f.g: Spread out along the wall, far apart.

n: So he gives a simple plan: when you hear the trumpet, rally to it, and God will fight for us. They would face trouble together, not alone.

f.w: our God shall fight for us

n: The work went on from dawn until the stars came out, with half of the men always on guard.

f.g: Until nightfall.

n: Workers from outside towns stay in Jerusalem overnight to serve as night guards. Everyone took a share of both labor and watching.
Nehemiah and his men never changed out of their clothes, staying ready at all times. The last phrase is hard to translate; many think it means each kept his weapon at hand, even when going for water.

f.w: saving that every one put them off for washing
f.g: The Hebrew is unclear; it may mean “each kept his weapon in his right hand” or “even at the water.”
